---
title: "String, `&str`, and Slices"
description: "One key Rust idea, one tiny executable example, the reason it works, and a precise pitfall."
---

## The question

**Why should a function usually accept `&str` instead of taking an owned String?**

`String` owns and can grow its UTF-8 bytes. `&str` is a borrowed view of a valid UTF-8 string slice. Taking `&str` makes a function usable with both a String and string literals.

## The core rule

Borrow the part you need, not an unnecessary copy of the whole allocation.

## One complete example

Paste these lines into `main.rs` and run with `rustc --edition 2024 main.rs && ./main`, or [use the tested Rust examples project](examples/index.qmd).

~~~rust
fn first_word(s: &str) -> &str {
    s.split_whitespace().next().unwrap_or("")
}
fn main() {
    let sentence = String::from("hello world");
    println!("{}", first_word(&sentence)); // hello
}
~~~

**Walk through it:** The `first_word` function reads through a `&str`; it neither clones nor moves the `String`. The returned slice refers to the existing text and cannot safely outlive that text.

## Common misunderstanding

Strings are UTF-8: indexing `s[0]` is not allowed because a byte index is not necessarily a Unicode character boundary. Distinguish bytes, `chars()`, and grapheme clusters.

## Remember it in one sentence

Borrow the part you need, not an unnecessary copy of the whole allocation.

**Official reference:** [The Rust Programming Language / Rust Reference](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch04-03-slices.html).
